note: Bought with excitement, used less and less, then left on a shelf. Tests absence and what a neglected droid inherits.
label: a droid that got shelved

moments_per_day.source: Bentley et al. 2018, IMWUT 2(3) Art. 91, Table 6, light-user cluster: 2.30 sessions/day, 2.61 commands/day
moments_per_day.note: Picking the light-user cluster is part of the scenario. Before shelving

weekend.source: Bentley et al. 2018, IMWUT 2(3) Art. 91, Table 6: light users gave 23% of use on weekends

novelty.peak.source: Cagiltay et al. 2022 (IDC), Misty II, 14 homes
novelty.peak.note: Only measured magnitude: weekly use fell about 2.2x from week 1 to week 4 (Table 1, converting 'once a week'=1, 'a few times'=3, 'daily'=7). The conversion is an interpretation and the robot was a children's reading tutor, so the range is kept wide and swept

novelty.days.source: Weiss et al. 2021 (RO-MAN, Anki Vector): attachment dropped after 2 weeks · Bajones et al. 2019: novelty passed by 3 weeks · Cagiltay et al. 2022: still declining in week 4

long_term.floor.source: Shen & Guan 2025 (国际新闻界 2025(2)), 47 homes, 9 months: no older adult used the robot past 6 months, and a robot kept on display counted as abandoned
long_term.floor.derivation: 0 of 47 homes still interacting after 6 months, so the floor is 0

long_term.from_day.source: Shen & Guan 2025: 15 of 47 used it less after 1 to 2 months

long_term.to_day.source: Shen & Guan 2025: 19 of 47 used it on and off for 2 to 3 months, then stopped

mix.source: Defines this household. No study measures how often people wave at, praise or insult a companion robot
mix.note: Results are conditional: 'in a home where moments look like this'. Only the proportions matter. Replace with real playtest proportions after week 10
